title: Noise in Single-Stage Amplifiers
intro: With input-referred noise in hand, each basic stage reduces to a short formula. The recurring lesson: devices that convert the input voltage to current should have a large $g_m$; devices that only supply bias current should have a small one.

blocks.text: A useful lemma

A drain noise current $\overline{I_n^2}$ is equivalent to a gate voltage $\overline{V_n^2} = \overline{I_n^2}/g_m^2$, for any source impedance at the gate (at low frequencies): both give the same output short-circuit current, $I_n/[Z_S(g_m + g_{mb} + 1/r_o) + 1]$. So $4kT\gamma/g_m$ is just the channel noise moved to the gate.
Common-source stage

blocks.alt: Common-source stage with a noise current source of 4kT over RD across the load resistor and a noise current source of 4kT gamma gm across M1's drain and source.
blocks.caption: Both noise currents flow into the load.

items: Current-source load M2: both drain currents flow into $r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2}$, giving $\overline{V_{n,in}^2} = 4kT\gamma\left(\frac{1}{g_{m1}} + \frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}^2}\right)$. The output noise of M1 rises as $\sqrt{g_{m1}}$ while the gain rises as $g_{m1}$, so a larger $g_{m1}$ helps; M2 only adds noise, so keep $g_{m2}$ small (a large overdrive).

Complementary stage (NMOS and PMOS both driven): same output noise, but gain $(g_{m1} + g_{m2})(r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2})$, so $\overline{V_{n,in}^2} = 4kT\gamma/(g_{m1} + g_{m2})$. Here M2 amplifies as well as adding noise.

Resistor plus PMOS current source in parallel as the load: $\overline{V_{n,in}^2} = 4kT\gamma\left(\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}^2} + \frac{1}{g_{m1}}\right) + \frac{1}{C_{ox}f}\left[\frac{K_Pg_{m2}^2}{(WL)_2g_{m1}^2} + \frac{K_N}{(WL)_1}\right] + \frac{4kT}{g_{m1}^2R_D}$.

blocks.text: With $g_m = 2I_D/(V_{GS} - V_{TH})$, the resistive-load result becomes

For a fixed drop $I_DR_D$ (headroom) and fixed overdrive, raising $I_D$ (and width with it) lowers the noise: noise is bought with current. For flicker noise the lever is area: scaling $W$ and $L$ together keeps $g_m$ and thermal noise but cuts 1/f noise, at the cost of capacitance. (A tempting argument that the drain flicker current is independent of $W$ fails because it lets the overdrive change; at fixed $I_D$ and overdrive it falls as $1/(WL)$.)
Integrated output noise and SNR
With a load capacitance, the output noise is shaped by the output pole. For the current-source-loaded stage, using the kT/C integral,

for a sinusoid of peak $V_m$. The SNR improves with $C_L$, that is, with less bandwidth: broadband low-noise design is hard. For a resistive load the same integration gives $\overline{V_{n,out,tot}^2} = (1 + \gamma g_mR_D)\,kT/C_L$; dividing by $(g_mR_D)^2$ and fixing the bandwidth $1/(2\pi R_DC_L)$ ties $g_m$ and $R_D$ to an rms noise target, and the bias current and headroom must then be checked.
Common-gate stage
The input impedance is low, so the input noise current matters even at low frequencies. Shorting the input:

With the input open, M1's own noise current has nowhere to go but back through M1 (its drain current must cancel it), so only $R_D$ reaches the output: the load noise is referred to the input without any reduction, because the stage has no current gain. The bias source matters too:

blocks.alt: Common-gate stage: M1 with gate at Vb1, drain to RD and the output, source at the input node. Below it, M2 with gate at Vb2 is the bias current source, with a noise current source of 4kT gamma gm2 in parallel.
blocks.caption: The bias device's noise adds directly to the input noise current.

blocks.text: Its noise current flows into a shorted input, adding no voltage noise, but with the input open it all flows through M1 into $R_D$: it adds $4kT\gamma g_{m2}$ to $\overline{I_{n,in}^2}$. Keep $g_{m2}$ small, which means a large overdrive and less headroom. With PMOS current-source load M3 and NMOS bias M2 (all saturated), $\overline{V_{n,in}^2} = 4kT\gamma(g_{m1} + g_{m3})/(g_{m1} + g_{mb1})^2$ and $\overline{I_{n,in}^2} \approx 4kT\gamma(g_{m2} + g_{m3})$. Flicker noise of M2 and M3 adds to the input current in the same way, and a diode-connected bias reference adds noise too unless filtered (see the current mirror page).
Source follower
The input impedance is high, so only the voltage source matters. With current-source bias M2:
the same as a CS stage with a current-source load, but with a gain below one; followers are avoided in low-noise signal paths.
Cascode

At low frequencies the cascode device adds almost nothing: its noise current must flow back through itself (M1's drain impedance is high), or, using the lemma, its gate noise sees little gain through the high impedance at node X. So $\overline{V_{n,in}^2} \approx 4kT(\gamma/g_{m1} + 1/(g_{m1}^2R_D))$. At high frequencies the capacitance $C_X$ gives M2's noise a path: $V_{n,out}/V_{n2} \approx -R_D/[1/g_{m2} + 1/(C_Xs)]$, while $C_X$ also steals signal current, so the input-referred noise rises. With a very high load resistance (a cascode load) the gain from M2's gate noise grows, but the signal gain grows more, so it stays negligible.
Noise bandwidth

To compare circuits with the same low-frequency noise but different roll-offs, use the noise bandwidth: the width of a brick-wall filter with the same total noise. For one pole it is $(\pi/2)f_p$. See the noise-power and bandwidth page.
Worked problems

blocks.title: CS stage input noise
blocks.text: $g_m = 2\text{ mS}$, $R_D = 10\text{ k}\Omega$, $\gamma = 2/3$. Find the input-referred thermal noise density at 300 K.
blocks.answer: About $2.4\text{ nV}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$, mostly from the transistor.

blocks.title: Load choice
blocks.text: An input device has $g_{m1} = 4\text{ mS}$ and $\gamma = 1$. Compare the input thermal noise with (a) a PMOS current-source load of $g_{m2} = 1\text{ mS}$, (b) the same PMOS driven as a complementary stage.
solution: M1 alone would give $2.03\text{ nV}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$: the passive load adds noise, the driven one removes some.

blocks.title: Integrated noise and SNR
blocks.text: A resistively loaded CS stage has $g_m = 5\text{ mS}$, $R_D = 2\text{ k}\Omega$, $C_L = 0.5\text{ pF}$, $\gamma = 1$. Find the bandwidth, the total output noise, the input-referred total, and the SNR for a 10 mV peak input sinusoid.
solution: $\overline{V_{n,out,tot}^2} = (1 + \gamma g_mR_D)kT/C_L = 11 \times 4.14 \times 10^{-21}/5 \times 10^{-13} = 9.1 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{V}^2$, i.e. $302\ \mu\text{V}$ rms. Divided by the gain: $30\ \mu\text{V}$ at the input.
Signal power at the output: $(10 \times 10\text{ mV})^2/2 = 5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{V}^2$. SNR $= 5 \times 10^{-3}/9.1 \times 10^{-8} = 5.5 \times 10^4$, or 47.4 dB.
blocks.answer: 159 MHz; 302 µV rms out (30 µV input-referred); SNR 47 dB.

blocks.title: Common-gate noise current
blocks.text: A CG stage has $g_m = 5\text{ mS}$, $g_m + g_{mb} = 6\text{ mS}$, $R_D = 2\text{ k}\Omega$, $\gamma = 1$, and a bias device with $g_{m2} = 2\text{ mS}$. Find $V_{n,in}$ and $I_{n,in}$.
solution: $\overline{I_{n,in}^2} = 4kT/R_D + 4kT\gamma g_{m2} = 4kT(5 \times 10^{-4} + 2 \times 10^{-3})$, so $6.43\text{ pA}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ (2.88 pA/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ without the bias device).
